items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The presence of social justice and the attitudes, institutions and structures that create and sustain peaceful societies, so that structural and cultural violence are also absent (Galtung)"?
items.answer: positive peace
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of positive peace.

items.stem: Distinguish between negative peace and positive peace.
items.answer: Negative peace is the absence of direct violence; positive peace is the presence of social justice and structures that meet human needs, so that structural and cultural violence are also absent.
items.markingKey: Negative peace is the absence of direct violence; positive peace is the presence of social justice and structures that meet human needs, so that structural and cultural violence are also absent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why Galtung argued that the absence of war is not enough to define peace.
items.answer: Societies without fighting can still contain structural violence – poverty, discrimination and exclusion that shorten lives – and cultural violence that legitimises it; real (positive) peace requires removing these through justice and equitable institutions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Societies without fighting can still contain structural violence – poverty, discrimination and exclusion that shorten lives – and cultural violence that legitimises it; real (positive) peace requires removing these through justice and equitable institutions. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source B
In many Latin American cities, homicide rates are higher than the death rates in some war zones. Yet because there is no war, these countries are counted as being at peace.
— UN Office on Drugs and Crime, Global Study on Homicide (2019) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source B, explain why the source challenges a narrow definition of peace. [3]
items.answer: It shows that the absence of war (negative peace in the interstate sense) can coexist with very high levels of direct violence, so defining peace only as the absence of war hides insecurity; a broader view of peace and violence is needed.
items.markingKey: It shows that the absence of war (negative peace in the interstate sense) can coexist with very high levels of direct violence, so defining peace only as the absence of war hides insecurity; a broader view of peace and violence is needed. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: "Positive peace is simply a long period of negative peace." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Positive peace is qualitatively different: it concerns justice, equity and institutions, not just the duration of the absence of war.
items.markingKey: Positive peace is qualitatively different: it concerns justice, equity and institutions, not just the duration of the absence of war. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Discuss the view that peace cannot exist without justice. [15]
items.answer: Lasting peace requires justice, but in the short term negotiated peace may require compromises on justice.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: Galtung’s positive peace; South Africa’s transition and the TRC; peace without justice: authoritarian stability; justice demands can prolong conflict (ICC warrants). Possible judgement: Lasting peace requires justice, but in the short term negotiated peace may require compromises on justice. items.stem: "A peace that rests on military deterrence is not a genuine peace." Discuss.
items.answer: Deterrence can secure negative peace, which matters, but it is not positive peace unless accompanied by justice and cooperation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Cold War “long peace” in Europe rested on fear of nuclear war; deterrence leaves structural and cultural violence untouched (Korea since 1953); arms races and security dilemmas persist. Arguments against: deterrence has prevented great-power war since 1945; negative peace saves lives and allows institutions to develop; Western Europe moved from deterrence to integration (EU). Supported judgement: Deterrence can secure negative peace, which matters, but it is not positive peace unless accompanied by justice and cooperation. items.stem: Explain why a ceasefire may produce negative peace without positive peace.
items.answer: A ceasefire stops the fighting but leaves the grievances, inequalities and hostile narratives that caused the conflict untouched, as on the Korean peninsula since 1953 or in Cyprus since 1974, so the risk of renewed violence remains.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the concept of positive peace has been criticised.
items.answer: Critics argue it is so broad that almost any social problem becomes “violence”, weakening the concept analytically and making it hard to use for policy; realists also see it as utopian.

items.stem: With reference to Costa Rica after abolishing its army in 1948–49, explain how it illustrates positive peace.
items.answer: Costa Rica abolished its armed forces under José Figueres and redirected spending to education and health; it has remained stable and democratic. Investment in social institutions rather than the military illustrates the building of structures that sustain peace beyond the absence of war.
items.markingKey: Context (Costa Rica abolished its armed forces under José Figueres and redirected spending to education and health; it has remained stable and democratic.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Investment in social institutions rather than the military illustrates the building of structures that sustain peace beyond the absence of war. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to positive peace.

— Institute for Economics and Peace, Positive Peace Report (2022) (adapted)

With reference to Source D, explain how the source reflects Galtung’s distinction between negative and positive peace. [4]
items.answer: The source rejects a definition of peace as the absence of war (negative peace) and defines it through attitudes, institutions and structures, which corresponds to Galtung’s positive peace – the removal of structural causes of violence and the presence of justice.

items.stem: "Positive peace is a more useful concept than negative peace for understanding contemporary conflict." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Positive peace is more useful for explaining and preventing conflict, but negative peace remains the essential first step.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: most conflicts are intrastate and rooted in structural grievances; explains violence in societies “at peace” (homicide, discrimination); guides peacebuilding (institutions, justice). Arguments against: negative peace is measurable and a precondition for anything else; positive peace is broad and value-laden; ending killing (ceasefires) is the immediate priority in war zones. Supported judgement: Positive peace is more useful for explaining and preventing conflict, but negative peace remains the essential first step. items.stem: Briefly explain why structural violence is often described as “invisible”.
items.answer: It is built into institutions and social arrangements rather than committed by an identifiable person at a specific time, so its harm (shorter lives, malnutrition) appears normal or natural.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Rwandan genocide (1994) shows the link between cultural and direct violence.
items.answer: Around 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu were killed in about 100 days, after years of propaganda by media such as RTLM and Kangura. Dehumanising propaganda (cultural violence) normalised hatred and helped mobilise ordinary people to commit mass killing (direct violence).

Source D
Direct violence is an event; structural violence is a process, with ups and downs; cultural violence is an invariant, a permanence, remaining essentially the same for long periods.
— Johan Galtung, “Cultural Violence”, Journal of Peace Research (1990) (extract)

Using evidence from Source D, explain how the source helps to explain why some conflicts recur. [4]
items.answer: If cultural violence is a slow-changing permanence and structural violence an ongoing process, then ending a violent event (direct violence) leaves the underlying forms intact, so violence can recur unless structures and cultures are transformed.

items.answer: Direct violence has an identifiable perpetrator and visible victims (e.g. a massacre); structural violence results from social and economic structures that harm people indirectly (e.g. avoidable deaths from lack of health care) without a single perpetrator.

items.stem: "Structural violence causes more harm than direct violence in the contemporary world." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Structural violence probably causes more cumulative harm, but the two are intertwined and direct violence is more immediately destructive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: millions of avoidable deaths from poverty and lack of health care each year; inequality shortens life expectancy (e.g. within and between states); structural violence underlies many armed conflicts. Arguments against: direct violence in war causes immediate mass casualties (e.g. Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine); the concept is hard to measure, so comparisons are uncertain; direct violence destroys the structures needed to reduce poverty. Supported judgement: Structural violence probably causes more cumulative harm, but the two are intertwined and direct violence is more immediately destructive. items.answer: They attract wider participation (women, the elderly, children), which raises the costs of repression, encourages defections among security forces and elites, and preserves international legitimacy, as Chenoweth and Stephan argue.

items.answer: It is an active strategy of confrontation, using strikes, boycotts and civil disobedience to impose costs on opponents and withdraw cooperation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the People Power Revolution in the Philippines (1986) and explain what it reveals about the effectiveness of non-violent resistance.
items.answer: After a fraudulent election, about two million people gathered on EDSA in Manila; soldiers defected and Ferdinand Marcos fled into exile. Mass, peaceful participation encouraged military defections and removed a dictator without civil war.
items.markingKey: Context (After a fraudulent election, about two million people gathered on EDSA in Manila; soldiers defected and Ferdinand Marcos fled into exile.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Source A
Non-violent resistance campaigns were nearly twice as likely to achieve full or partial success as their violent counterparts. This is because they attract far larger and more diverse participation, which raises the costs of repression and makes defections from the regime more likely.
— Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan, Why Civil Resistance Works (2011) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source A, explain why mass participation matters to the success of non-violent movements. [4]
items.answer: The source links success to participation: large and diverse movements impose economic and political costs (strikes, boycotts), make repression of ordinary citizens harder to justify, and increase the chance that soldiers and elites with links to protesters defect.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Non-violent resistance is the most effective way for citizens to challenge state power."
items.answer: Non-violence is generally more effective, but its success depends on mass participation, security force defection and regime type.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Chenoweth and Stephan’s data (53% vs 26% success); People Power 1986, Otpor 2000, Sudan 2019; retains legitimacy and broad participation. Arguments against: success rates have fallen since 2010 as regimes adapt (digital surveillance, Myanmar 2021); violent movements have achieved independence (Algeria 1962); outcomes may be reversed by militaries (Egypt 2013, Sudan 2021). Supported judgement: Non-violence is generally more effective, but its success depends on mass participation, security force defection and regime type.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Sudanese revolution (2018–2019) and explain what it reveals about the possibilities and limits of non-violence.
items.answer: Protests organised by the Sudanese Professionals Association led to the removal of Omar al-Bashir in April 2019; the June 2019 Khartoum massacre killed over 100 protesters. Non-violent mobilisation removed a long-standing ruler, but the military retained power and staged a coup in 2021, showing that transitions can be reversed.

items.stem:
Source A
In many Latin American cities, homicide rates are higher than the death rates in some war zones. Yet because there is no war, these countries are counted as being at peace.
— UN Office on Drugs and Crime, Global Study on Homicide (2019) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source A, explain why the source challenges a narrow definition of peace. [4]
items.answer: It shows that the absence of war (negative peace in the interstate sense) can coexist with very high levels of direct violence, so defining peace only as the absence of war hides insecurity; a broader view of peace and violence is needed.
items.markingKey: It shows that the absence of war (negative peace in the interstate sense) can coexist with very high levels of direct violence, so defining peace only as the absence of war hides insecurity; a broader view of peace and violence is needed. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: "Structural violence causes more harm than direct violence in the contemporary world." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Structural violence probably causes more cumulative harm, but the two are intertwined and direct violence is more immediately destructive.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: millions of avoidable deaths from poverty and lack of health care each year; inequality shortens life expectancy (e.g. within and between states); structural violence underlies many armed conflicts. Arguments against: direct violence in war causes immediate mass casualties (e.g. Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine); the concept is hard to measure, so comparisons are uncertain; direct violence destroys the structures needed to reduce poverty. Possible judgement: Structural violence probably causes more cumulative harm, but the two are intertwined and direct violence is more immediately destructive. items.stem: Examine the view that non-violent resistance is the most effective way for citizens to challenge state power. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Non-violence is generally more effective, but its success depends on mass participation, security force defection and regime type.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: Chenoweth and Stephan’s data (53% vs 26% success); People Power 1986, Otpor 2000, Sudan 2019; retains legitimacy and broad participation. Arguments against: success rates have fallen since 2010 as regimes adapt (digital surveillance, Myanmar 2021); violent movements have achieved independence (Algeria 1962); outcomes may be reversed by militaries (Egypt 2013, Sudan 2021). Possible judgement: Non-violence is generally more effective, but its success depends on mass participation, security force defection and regime type. items.stem: "Positive peace is a more useful concept than negative peace for understanding contemporary conflict." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Positive peace is more useful for explaining and preventing conflict, but negative peace remains the essential first step.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: most conflicts are intrastate and rooted in structural grievances; explains violence in societies “at peace” (homicide, discrimination); guides peacebuilding (institutions, justice). Arguments against: negative peace is measurable and a precondition for anything else; positive peace is broad and value-laden; ending killing (ceasefires) is the immediate priority in war zones. Possible judgement: Positive peace is more useful for explaining and preventing conflict, but negative peace remains the essential first step. items.stem: To what extent is Galtung’s violence triangle useful for understanding a contemporary conflict you have studied? [15]
items.answer: The triangle is a useful diagnostic tool, but it must be combined with analysis of actors, interests and power.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: direct, structural and cultural violence in Myanmar (Rohingya); how cultural narratives legitimise exclusion; limits: actors and interests (greed) under-explained; broadness of the concept. Possible judgement: The triangle is a useful diagnostic tool, but it must be combined with analysis of actors, interests and power. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Positive Peace Index".
items.answer: The Institute for Economics and Peace measure of the attitudes, institutions and structures (eight “pillars”, e.g. well-functioning government, low corruption, equitable distribution of resources) that sustain peace
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the Institute for Economics and Peace measure of the attitudes, institutions and structures (eight “pillars”, e.g. well-functioning government, low corruption, equitable distribution of resources) that sustain peace. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Galtung’s model showing direct violence as the visible tip, with structural and cultural violence as the invisible forms that sustain it"?
items.answer: violence triangle
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of violence triangle.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "3.5 per cent rule"?
options: The Institute for Economics and Peace measure of the attitudes, institutions and structures (eight “pillars”, e.g. well-functioning government, low corruption, equitable distribution of resources) that sustain peace
Visible physical or psychological harm inflicted by an identifiable actor, such as killing, torture or assault
The use of methods such as protests, strikes, boycotts and civil disobedience, without the use or threat of violence, to achieve political change
Erica Chenoweth’s finding that no campaign which mobilised at least 3.5 per cent of the population in sustained protest failed in the period studied
items.answer: Erica Chenoweth’s finding that no campaign which mobilised at least 3.5 per cent of the population in sustained protest failed in the period studied
items.markingKey: D. "3.5 per cent rule" is Erica Chenoweth’s finding that no campaign which mobilised at least 3.5 per cent of the population in sustained protest failed in the period studied.

items.stem: "A country that is not at war is at peace in every meaningful sense." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It may enjoy negative peace while suffering structural violence (poverty, discrimination) and high levels of interpersonal violence, so it lacks positive peace.
items.markingKey: It may enjoy negative peace while suffering structural violence (poverty, discrimination) and high levels of interpersonal violence, so it lacks positive peace. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the violence triangle is useful for peacebuilding.
items.answer: It shows that ending direct violence is not enough: structural (inequality, exclusion) and cultural (narratives, prejudice) forms must also be addressed, or violence will recur.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows that ending direct violence is not enough: structural (inequality, exclusion) and cultural (narratives, prejudice) forms must also be addressed, or violence will recur. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Non-violent movements only succeed against democratic governments." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Non-violent campaigns have toppled authoritarian regimes, such as the People Power revolution in the Philippines (1986) and the Serbian Otpor movement against Milošević (2000).
items.markingKey: Non-violent campaigns have toppled authoritarian regimes, such as the People Power revolution in the Philippines (1986) and the Serbian Otpor movement against Milošević (2000). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Positive peace is simply a long period of negative peace." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Positive peace is qualitatively different: it concerns justice, equity and institutions, not just the duration of the absence of war.
items.markingKey: Positive peace is qualitatively different: it concerns justice, equity and institutions, not just the duration of the absence of war. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between direct violence and structural violence.
items.answer: Direct violence has an identifiable perpetrator and visible victims (e.g. a massacre); structural violence results from social and economic structures that harm people indirectly (e.g. avoidable deaths from lack of health care) without a single perpetrator.
items.markingKey: Direct violence has an identifiable perpetrator and visible victims (e.g. a massacre); structural violence results from social and economic structures that harm people indirectly (e.g. avoidable deaths from lack of health care) without a single perpetrator. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Non-violent resistance is a passive way of accepting injustice." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It is an active strategy of confrontation, using strikes, boycotts and civil disobedience to impose costs on opponents and withdraw cooperation.
items.markingKey: It is an active strategy of confrontation, using strikes, boycotts and civil disobedience to impose costs on opponents and withdraw cooperation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Costa Rica after abolishing its army in 1948–49 shows positive peace.
items.answer: Costa Rica abolished its armed forces under José Figueres and redirected spending to education and health; it has remained stable and democratic. Investment in social institutions rather than the military illustrates the building of structures that sustain peace beyond the absence of war.
items.markingKey: Context (Costa Rica abolished its armed forces under José Figueres and redirected spending to education and health; it has remained stable and democratic.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Investment in social institutions rather than the military illustrates the building of structures that sustain peace beyond the absence of war. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to positive peace.

items.stem: With reference to the use of sexual violence in the Bosnian war (1992–1995), explain how it illustrates gender-based violence as a weapon of war.
items.answer: Tens of thousands of women were raped, often systematically; the ICTY convicted perpetrators of rape as a crime against humanity in the Foča case (2001). Rape was used deliberately to terrorise communities and destroy group identity, showing violence directed at people because of their gender and ethnicity.
items.markingKey: Context (Tens of thousands of women were raped, often systematically; the ICTY convicted perpetrators of rape as a crime against humanity in the Foča case (2001).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rape was used deliberately to terrorise communities and destroy group identity, showing violence directed at people because of their gender and ethnicity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to gender-based violence as a weapon of war.

items.stem:
Source C
Non-violent resistance campaigns were nearly twice as likely to achieve full or partial success as their violent counterparts. This is because they attract far larger and more diverse participation, which raises the costs of repression and makes defections from the regime more likely.
— Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan, Why Civil Resistance Works (2011) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source C, explain why mass participation matters to the success of non-violent movements. [4]
items.answer: The source links success to participation: large and diverse movements impose economic and political costs (strikes, boycotts), make repression of ordinary citizens harder to justify, and increase the chance that soldiers and elites with links to protesters defect.
items.markingKey: The source links success to participation: large and diverse movements impose economic and political costs (strikes, boycotts), make repression of ordinary citizens harder to justify, and increase the chance that soldiers and elites with links to protesters defect. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem:
Source B
Peace is not merely the absence of war. We define positive peace as the attitudes, institutions and structures that create and sustain peaceful societies. Countries with high levels of positive peace are more resilient to shocks, recover faster and are less likely to fall into conflict.
— Institute for Economics and Peace, Positive Peace Report (2022) (adapted)

Outline three points made in Source B about the meaning of peace. [3]
items.answer: peace is more than the absence of war; positive peace consists of attitudes, institutions and structures; countries with high positive peace are more resilient and less likely to fall into conflict
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: peace is more than the absence of war; positive peace consists of attitudes, institutions and structures; countries with high positive peace are more resilient and less likely to fall into conflict. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: Using apartheid South Africa in the 1970s as an example, explain structural violence within negative peace.
items.answer: Apartheid laws enforced racial segregation in housing, education and employment, while the country was not at war with any state. Legal and economic structures systematically harmed the Black majority even without open war, showing how structural violence persists in apparent peace.
items.markingKey: Context (Apartheid laws enforced racial segregation in housing, education and employment, while the country was not at war with any state.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Legal and economic structures systematically harmed the Black majority even without open war, showing how structural violence persists in apparent peace. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to structural violence within negative peace.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Structural violence causes more harm than direct violence in the contemporary world."
items.answer: Structural violence probably causes more cumulative harm, but the two are intertwined and direct violence is more immediately destructive.

Supported judgement: Structural violence probably causes more cumulative harm, but the two are intertwined and direct violence is more immediately destructive.

items.stem: Discuss the factors that determine whether non-violent movements achieve their goals. [15]
items.answer: Participation and security-force defections are the decisive factors, though regime strategies increasingly limit success.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: scale and diversity of participation; security force loyalty; international support; regime type and use of technology for repression. Possible judgement: Participation and security-force defections are the decisive factors, though regime strategies increasingly limit success. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "A peace that rests on military deterrence is not a genuine peace."
items.answer: Deterrence can secure negative peace, which matters, but it is not positive peace unless accompanied by justice and cooperation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Cold War “long peace” in Europe rested on fear of nuclear war; deterrence leaves structural and cultural violence untouched (Korea since 1953); arms races and security dilemmas persist. Arguments against: deterrence has prevented great-power war since 1945; negative peace saves lives and allows institutions to develop; Western Europe moved from deterrence to integration (EU). Supported judgement: Deterrence can secure negative peace, which matters, but it is not positive peace unless accompanied by justice and cooperation. items.stem:
Source A
Direct violence is an event; structural violence is a process, with ups and downs; cultural violence is an invariant, a permanence, remaining essentially the same for long periods.
— Johan Galtung, “Cultural Violence”, Journal of Peace Research (1990) (extract)

With reference to Source A, explain how the source helps to explain why some conflicts recur. [4]
items.answer: If cultural violence is a slow-changing permanence and structural violence an ongoing process, then ending a violent event (direct violence) leaves the underlying forms intact, so violence can recur unless structures and cultures are transformed.
items.markingKey: If cultural violence is a slow-changing permanence and structural violence an ongoing process, then ending a violent event (direct violence) leaves the underlying forms intact, so violence can recur unless structures and cultures are transformed. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.
